title: "Expectation-Maximization"
description: "An iterative algorithm for estimating model parameters when data includes latent variables."
term: "Expectation-Maximization"

## Simple explanation

Expectation-maximization (EM) is an iterative method for estimating
parameters when a model includes hidden or missing variables. It
alternates between estimating those hidden variables and updating the
model parameters.

## Technical explanation

For observed data $X$, latent variables $Z$, and parameters $\theta$,
the E-step computes an expectation of the complete-data log-likelihood
under the current parameter estimate. The M-step chooses updated
parameters that maximize this expected quantity. Under standard
conditions, each iteration does not decrease the observed-data
likelihood, but it may converge to a local optimum.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

EM provides a principled way to fit latent-variable models and handle
incomplete data. It appears in mixture models and other statistical
methods, though its convergence and computational cost depend on the
model.

## How it works

Initialize parameters. In the E-step, estimate a distribution over latent
variables using the current parameters. In the M-step, update parameters
using those estimates. Repeat until a convergence criterion or iteration
limit is reached.

## Practical example

In a Gaussian mixture model, the E-step estimates each data point's
probability of belonging to each cluster. The M-step updates each
Gaussian's weights, means, and variances using those soft assignments.

## Common misconceptions

- EM does not generally guarantee a global optimum.
- The E-step estimates a distribution over latent variables; it does not
  necessarily assign each point to one cluster.
- Convergence of the objective does not guarantee that the fitted model
  is appropriate for the data.
